records.name: Grosvenor family (Dukes of Westminster)
records.scaleNote: Sunday Times Rich List 2026 puts the Duke of Westminster and family at £9.677bn (18th, richest hereditary peer); Grosvenor Group's 2025 accounts show £9.5bn of property assets under management.
records.lifespan: Eaton, Cheshire from the 1440s; Mayfair from 1677; present
records.origins: A Cheshire gentry family seated at Eaton since the early 1440s, which claims descent from a Norman knight, Gilbert le Grosveneur. The decisive step came in 1677, when Sir Thomas Grosvenor, 3rd Baronet, married the twelve-year-old Mary Davies, heiress to the manor of Ebury: meadow, marsh and pasture west of the City of London that became Mayfair, Belgravia and Pimlico.
records.role_summary: The fortune is a marriage turned into ground rent. From 1720 the Grosvenors laid out Mayfair around Grosvenor Square and from the 1820s Belgravia, granting long building leases and keeping the freehold, so rents and lease premiums came back to the family for three centuries. From 1952 the capital was spread abroad (Vancouver, Australia, Asia, continental Europe) and since 2012 into food and agricultural technology, all run by Grosvenor Group for family trusts.

roleDetail.d: Grosvenor's own history says the line goes back to Gilbert le Grosveneur, who came over with William the Conqueror; no Domesday entry or peerage authority found in this research confirms the link.
Sir Thomas Grosvenor married Mary Davies, heiress to the manor of Ebury, bringing the land that became Mayfair and Belgravia (Grosvenor history).
Development began in 1720; Mayfair's street grid largely survives. The family kept the freehold and let plots on long building leases.
Robert Grosvenor, later 1st Marquess of Westminster (1831), developed Belgravia south-west of Mayfair.
First major overseas investment at Annacis Island, Vancouver (1952), followed by Australia in the 1960s, Asia Pacific in 1994 and continental Europe in 1996; Liverpool ONE opened in 2008.

records.legacy: Grosvenor Group Limited, a UK company 'wholly owned by Trustees of the Grosvenor Trusts who hold the shares for the benefit of current and future generations of the Grosvenor family headed by the Duke of Westminster' (2025 accounts), runs c. 300 acres of Mayfair and Belgravia, property in the Americas, Asia and Europe, and a food and agtech arm. The Eaton estate and other rural estates sit alongside it.

legacyDetail.d: In January 2025 the group sold 24.99% of its Mayfair estate partnership to Norges Bank Investment Management for £304m gross, keeping control and management of the 175 properties (2025 accounts).
The shareholders are the Trustees of the Grosvenor Trusts; non-executive directors represent them on the board (2025 accounts).

norman.text: The family's claimed descent from Gilbert le Grosveneur, a companion of William I, rests on family tradition stated in Grosvenor's own history. This research found no Domesday or Complete Peerage confirmation; the documented line begins with the Cheshire Grosvenors of the 14th–15th centuries.

records.name: Cadogan family (Earls Cadogan)
records.scaleNote: Sunday Times Rich List 2026: Earl Cadogan and family £6.418bn (29th); the Chelsea portfolio was valued at £5.7bn at end-2024.
records.origins: Sir Hans Sloane, physician in Jamaica in 1687–89, married the widow of a Jamaican planter in 1695 and drew income from her sugar estates; in 1712 he bought the manor of Chelsea. In 1717 his daughter Elizabeth married Charles Cadogan, later 2nd Baron Cadogan, and the Sloane half of the Chelsea estate passed to the Cadogans.
records.role_summary: Cadogan is a single-district ground-rent fortune. The 1st Earl leased fields north of Chelsea to Henry Holland in the 1770s to build Hans Town (Sloane Street, Hans Place), and later earls rebuilt Cadogan Square and Sloane Street in red brick in the 1870s–90s on leases that reverted to the family. The estate still owns c. 93 acres of Chelsea and Knightsbridge freeholds, now worth about £5.7bn, and invests the income in retail, restaurants and, since 2025, regional property.

roleDetail.d: Historians cited by the London Society link Sloane's wife's Jamaican sugar income, worked by enslaved people, to his collecting and the 1712 Chelsea purchase.
Elizabeth Sloane's share of Chelsea passed to the Cadogans; the family still holds it.
Per UCL LBS, Charles Sloane Cadogan, later 1st Earl, lent £20,500 on a 320-acre Grenada estate and its enslaved people.
The estate's value now lies in Sloane Street, King's Road and Duke of York Square retail and residential lettings; the portfolio rose to £5.7bn in 2024.

records.legacy: The Chelsea estate is run by Cadogan Group Limited, owned through a chain of UK holding companies ending in Cadogan Settled Estates Shareholding Company Limited, which until 2025 named family trustees as persons with significant control. The family's wealth is the estate, held in settled trusts.

legacyDetail.t: A 2025 restructure of the top of the chain.
legacyDetail.d: In May 2025 two new companies, Cyfrwy Limited and Trychrug Ltd, became the registered controllers of Cadogan Settled Estates Holdings and the Shareholding Company, replacing four individual trustees.

records.name: Howard de Walden family (Marylebone estate; Holles–Harley–Portland–Ellis line)
records.scaleNote: Sunday Times Rich List 2026: Baron Howard de Walden and family £3.357bn (49th); Howard de Walden Estates reported net assets of £3.09bn at 31 March 2026.
records.origins: John Holles, Duke of Newcastle, bought the manor of Marylebone in 1708. It passed by marriage to the Harleys (Earls of Oxford) and in 1734 to the Bentinck Dukes of Portland, who developed it as the Portland Estate. When the 5th Duke of Portland died in 1879 it went to his sister Lucy, widow of the 6th Baron Howard de Walden, and so to the Ellis (later Scott-Ellis) family.
records.role_summary: An estate bought in 1708 and moved by three heiress marriages, then let on building leases: Harley Street, Wimpole Street, Cavendish Square and Portland Place were laid out in the 18th century, and the estate turned Harley Street into London's private medical district in the 20th. Rental income reached £179.4m in the year to March 2026.

roleDetail.d: Holles bought Marylebone; it passed through Henrietta Cavendish Holles (m. Edward Harley) and their daughter Margaret (m. 2nd Duke of Portland, 1734).
The Portland Estate's Marylebone part went to Lucy, Lady Howard de Walden, on her brother's death.
Per UCL LBS, Lord Seaford, father of the 6th Baron, was awarded c. £18,100 compensation for five Jamaican estates in the 1830s.
The estate built Harley Street into a private medical cluster and keeps the freeholds; rental income rose 9.3% to £179.4m in 2025/26.

records.legacy: Howard de Walden Estates Ltd owns c. 92 acres of Marylebone and is owned by the descendants of the four daughters of the 9th Baron (d. 1999). Peter Czernin, 11th Baron, succeeded in 2024.

legacyDetail.d: Investment properties £4.52bn, net assets £3.09bn, net debt £596.8m, pre-tax profit £335.8m including a £231.2m revaluation gain.

records.name: The Crown: Crown Estate, Duchy of Lancaster and Duchy of Cornwall (House of Windsor)
records.scaleNote: The Crown Estate's net asset value grew to £16.7bn in 2025/26 (as reported by The Independent); the King is listed personally at £680m (Rich List 2026, 230th).
records.lifespan: 1066–present (Duchy of Cornwall 1337; Duchy of Lancaster 1399; Crown Estate surrendered to Parliament 1760)
records.origins: After 1066 William I kept a large share of England as royal demesne, recorded as 'Land of the King' in Domesday (1086). Later kings added forfeited baronies, the Lancaster inheritance (1399) and monastic land seized in 1536–41, though much of it was granted or sold to courtiers.
records.role_summary: Three separate pots. The Crown Estate is the hereditary Crown land George III surrendered to Parliament in 1760 for a Civil List; its profits go to the Treasury and set the Sovereign Grant. The Duchy of Lancaster (since 1399) is the monarch's private income and the Duchy of Cornwall (since 1337) the heir's. In the 2020s the Crown Estate's monopoly over leasing the seabed for offshore wind became its biggest earner.

roleDetail.d: Domesday lists the king as the largest landholder; historians commonly put the royal share at about a fifth of recorded land value.
Edward III created the Duchy of Cornwall for his heir; the Duchy of Lancaster merged with the Crown when Henry IV took the throne in 1399.
George III gave the hereditary Crown lands' revenue to the Treasury in return for a Civil List, creating what became the Crown Estate.
Round 4 option fees lifted net revenue profit to £1.15bn in 2024/25; it fell back to c. £0.5bn (revenue account profit £487m) in 2025/26 as projects moved into construction.

records.legacy: The Crown Estate (England, Wales and Northern Ireland) is a statutory body that pays its profits to the Treasury. The Duchy of Lancaster funds the King's private income and the Duchy of Cornwall the Prince of Wales's. The King's personal fortune (Rich List: £680m) is separate from all three.

legacyDetail.d: The monarchy's core funding is calculated from Crown Estate profits; it was set at £132.1m for 2025/26.

legacyDetail.d: In 2017 the Paradise Papers showed the Duchy of Lancaster had invested about £10m in funds in the Cayman Islands and Bermuda, including Dover Street VI Cayman Fund LP; the Duchy said its investments were audited and legitimate.

norman.text: The royal demesne recorded in Domesday as 'Land of King William' is the documented root of Crown landholding; the present royal family descends from William I through several female lines.

records.scaleNote: The investment fund was valued at £11.6bn at end-2025 (8.0% return), making it one of the largest endowments in the UK.
records.origins: The Church held about a quarter of England's recorded land in 1086 and lost the monastic part at the Dissolution of 1536–41; the bishops' and cathedral estates survived. Queen Anne's Bounty (1704) used first-fruits and tenths to support poor clergy, and the Ecclesiastical Commissioners (1836) took over surplus bishops' and cathedral estates; the two were merged in 1948 as the Church Commissioners.
records.role_summary: A medieval landed endowment turned into a modern investment fund. Queen Anne's Bounty invested its spare cash almost exclusively in South Sea Company annuities from 1723 to 1777 (the Church's own research), while the Ecclesiastical Commissioners managed estates including what became the Hyde Park Estate in Paddington. Since the 1990s the fund has moved into equities, private equity and timberland while keeping rural and strategic land.

roleDetail.d: Commonly estimated at about a quarter of recorded land in 1086; this is a historians' estimate.

roleDetail.t: Queen Anne's Bounty and the South Sea Company.

records.name: William I and the Norman Conquest
records.scaleNote: Historians' estimates put the king's own share of Domesday-recorded land at roughly 17–20% and the Church's at about a quarter, of a total recorded value of c. £73,000 a year.
records.origins: Duke of Normandy from 1035, William claimed the English throne after Edward the Confessor's death and defeated Harold II at Hastings on 14 October 1066. Within twenty years almost every major English landholder had been replaced.
records.role_summary: The Conquest was the largest transfer of land in English history. William treated all land as held from the Crown: he kept a large royal demesne and granted the rest as fiefs to some 200 Norman barons and to churches, who sub-let to knights in return for military service. The Domesday survey of 1086 recorded who held what and what it was worth, so the Crown could tax and call on it.

roleDetail.d: Lands of English lords killed at Hastings or in later revolts were declared forfeit and regranted to William's followers.
Tenants-in-chief (roughly 1,400 people, mostly Normans, plus churches) held directly from the king; Open Domesday records them by name.
Estimates of the royal demesne range from about 17% to 20% of recorded land; English holders retained only a few per cent by 1086.
The survey listed 13,418 places, their holders in 1066 and 1086, resources and annual value.

records.legacy: Feudal tenure from the Crown is still the legal basis of English land law (all land is held of the Crown). Families such as the Percys, and institutions such as the Crown Estate and the Church, trace some holdings to the Conquest settlement, though most surviving great estates were made later, by Dissolution grants, marriages and urban development.

legacyDetail.d: Of the families in this project, only a few (Percy through heiresses; Shirley at Ettington; Berkeley, of English descent) can document a line back to 1086.

records.role_summary: A modest feudal fortune held for nine centuries rather than a great one made: manors held under the Ferrers honour, enlarged by marriage (Staunton Harold, Leicestershire), a baronetcy in 1611 and the earldom of Ferrers in 1711. The 4th Earl Ferrers was hanged at Tyburn for murdering his steward, the last peer to die a felon's death.

records.name: Berkeley family (Berkeley Castle)
records.scaleNote: The estate manages c. 6,000 acres of rural land and property (Berkeley Castle website); no published wealth figure.
records.origins: Robert Fitzharding, son of Harding, the king's reeve at Bristol, was a rich Bristol burgess who backed Henry of Anjou in the civil war; around 1153–54 Henry II granted him the barony of Berkeley and licence to rebuild the castle. He was very probably the grandson of Eadnoth the Staller, an English official of Edward the Confessor and Harold.
records.role_summary: Merchant capital turned into land: a Bristol financier's loans to the Angevin cause bought a Norman-era barony, which the family then held for nine centuries apart from 1492–1553, when William, Marquess Berkeley, settled the estates on Henry VII. Wealth came from feudal rents, the Severn vale's farms and fisheries, and later tourism; Edward II was murdered in the castle in 1327.

roleDetail.d: Henry II's charter allowed Robert Fitzharding to rebuild the castle at Berkeley; a Berkeley Castle charter is dated c. November 1153.
Descent from Eadnoth the Staller was called 'in the highest degree probable' by the historian E. A. Freeman; the family is cited as one of very few with a patrilineal Anglo-Saxon ancestor.
The castle was in royal hands from 1492 to 1553, then returned to the family.

records.legacy: Berkeley Castle and an estate of c. 6,000 acres in Gloucestershire and at Spetchley, Worcestershire, remain with the family; the castle is open to visitors under the Berkeley Castle Charitable Trust (charity 1061062). Charles Berkeley represents the family that has held it for nine centuries.

legacyDetail.d: The estate manages farmland, rivers, forestry and residential and commercial property, with weddings and events at the castle.

records.name: Death duties to inheritance tax (1894 estate duty → IHT; heritage, agricultural and business reliefs)
records.description: Estate duty, introduced in 1894, rose to 80% at the top by the 1940s and forced sales such as the Lowthers' West Cumberland estate (1955–59) and Hardwick Hall's transfer to the Treasury after the 10th Duke of Devonshire's death in 1950. Great estates responded by moving land into trusts, which pay periodic charges of up to 6% every ten years instead of 40% at death, and by relying on agricultural and business property relief; from 6 April 2026, 100% relief is capped at £2.5m of combined agricultural and business property per person and per trust, with 50% relief above.

sources.label: GOV.UK — Agricultural property relief and business property relief changes

Whitehaven News — Why the Lowthers sold up in West Cumbria

records.name: Register of Overseas Entities (2022)
records.description: Created by the Economic Crime (Transparency and Enforcement) Act 2022 and opened on 1 August 2022, the register requires non-UK entities that own UK land to name their registrable beneficial owners at Companies House. Trust information became available to applicants from 31 August 2025. It does not cover UK companies or UK trusts, which is how most great estates hold their land.

records.name: HM Land Registry corporate ownership datasets (CCOD and OCOD)
records.description: HM Land Registry publishes two free datasets of land titles in England and Wales owned by companies: UK companies (CCOD) and overseas companies (OCOD). They list title numbers, addresses and tenure but not beneficial owners, so they must be matched with Companies House and the Register of Overseas Entities; individuals' and trusts' land is not included.

records.name: Who Owns England? (Guy Shrubsole, 2019)
records.description: Campaigner Guy Shrubsole's book and website, built on Land Registry data, FOI requests and estate maps, estimated in 2019 that about half of England is owned by under 1% of the population. His breakdown: aristocracy and gentry c. 30%, corporations c. 18%, 'new money' c. 17%, public sector c. 8.5%, homeowners c. 5%, conservation charities c. 2%, the Crown c. 1.4% and the Church of England c. 0.5%, with c. 17% unregistered.

records.name: Bloomsbury estate (Bedford Estates)
records.description: Thomas Wriothesley, later Earl of Southampton, acquired Bloomsbury at the Dissolution in 1545; it passed to the Russells by Rachel Wriothesley's 1669 marriage and was developed with Bedford, Russell and Tavistock Squares. Twentieth-century sales cut it from 112 acres to about 20, still the largest private holding in Bloomsbury.

records.description: The unincorporated family settlement that owns the Devonshire estates (Chatsworth, Bolton Abbey, Compton Estate in Eastbourne, Lismore) and trades as 'the Devonshire Group', which is 'not a legal entity'. As a private trust it files no public balance sheet; the Chatsworth House Trust, a separate charity, runs the house.

events.title: Battle of Hastings
events.text: William of Normandy defeats Harold II on 14 October; the forfeiture of English lords' lands begins the largest land transfer in English history.

events.title: Domesday survey completed
events.text: The survey records c. 1,400 tenants-in-chief; William de Percy holds 141 places and Saswalo holds Ettington under Henry de Ferrers.

events.title: Robert Fitzharding granted Berkeley
events.text: Henry of Anjou rewards the Bristol financier with the barony and castle of Berkeley, held by the family ever since apart from 1492–1553.

events.title: Magna Carta
events.text: King John concedes limits on feudal reliefs, wardship and forest, protecting baronial inheritance against the Crown.

events.title: Duchy of Lancaster joins the Crown
events.text: Henry IV's accession unites the Lancaster inheritance with the Crown; it still funds the monarch's private income.

source.label: Duchy of Lancaster — Annual report and accounts year ended 31 March 2026

events.title: Tavistock Abbey granted to John Russell
events.text: The first of three monastic grants (Tavistock 1539, Woburn 1547, Covent Garden 1552) that founded the Bedford fortune.

source.label: UCL Bloomsbury Project — Estates in Bloomsbury

events.title: Longleat and Wilton pass to Tudor officials
events.text: Sir John Thynne buys Longleat Priory and William Herbert receives the Wilton Abbey estate after its 1539 surrender.

events.title: Robert Cecil receives Hatfield
events.text: James I takes Theobalds and gives Hatfield to his chief minister, who builds Hatfield House by 1612.

events.title: Bloomsbury comes to the Russells
events.text: Rachel Wriothesley, heiress to the Dissolution-era Bloomsbury estate, marries William, Lord Russell.

source.label: UCL Bloomsbury Project — Estates in Bloomsbury

events.title: Grosvenor–Davies marriage brings the manor of Ebury
events.text: Sir Thomas Grosvenor marries the heiress Mary Davies; her land becomes Mayfair and Belgravia.

events.title: Sloane's Chelsea passes to the Cadogans
events.text: Elizabeth Sloane marries Charles Cadogan; the Chelsea estate is still the Cadogan family's.

source.label: London Society — Chelsea, Sir Hans Sloane and the slavery connection

events.title: Marylebone heiress marries the Duke of Portland
events.text: Margaret Cavendish Harley brings Welbeck and Marylebone to the Bentincks.

events.title: George III surrenders the Crown lands
events.text: Hereditary Crown revenues are handed to Parliament for a Civil List, creating the Crown Estate.

source.label: GOV.UK — The Crown Estate Integrated Annual Report 2025 to 2026

events.title: Marylebone passes to the Howard de Waldens
events.text: The 5th Duke of Portland dies; the Marylebone estate goes to his sister Lucy, Lady Howard de Walden.

events.title: Estate duty introduced
events.text: Death duties on landed estates begin; by the 1940s top rates of 80% force sales and transfers in lieu.

source.label: Chartered Institute of Taxation — Behind the headlines on the Duke and all that money

events.title: Church Commissioners formed
events.text: Queen Anne's Bounty and the Ecclesiastical Commissioners merge into the Church Commissioners for England.

events.title: Devonshire death duties
events.text: The 10th Duke dies; duties at 80% (reported at £7m) lead to Hardwick Hall being accepted by the Treasury.

source.label: House and Heritage — How Chatsworth's treasures were cared for

events.title: 7th Duke of Westminster inherits through trusts
events.text: Hugh Grosvenor succeeds; because the estate is held in trusts, no single 40% inheritance tax charge applies, prompting calls for reform.

events.text: Leaked Appleby files show the Duchy of Lancaster invested about £10m in Cayman and Bermuda funds; the Duchy says the investments were audited and legitimate.

trails.title: From a Cheshire manor to Mayfair to Grosvenor Group and the trusts
trails.summary: A gentry family's marriage to a twelve-year-old heiress in 1677 brought pasture west of London that became Mayfair and Belgravia. Leasehold development turned it into ground rent, the rents were reinvested worldwide from 1952, and today trustees own a £4.2bn-equity property group that manages £9.5bn of assets.

steps.title: Seated at Eaton
steps.text: The Grosvenors, Cheshire gentry who claim descent from a Norman knight, settle at Eaton in the early 1440s.

steps.title: Marriage to Mary Davies
steps.text: Sir Thomas Grosvenor marries the heiress to the manor of Ebury: meadow, marsh and pasture west of the City.

steps.title: Mayfair laid out on building leases
steps.text: Development begins around Grosvenor Square; builders take long leases and the family keeps the freehold and the reversion.

steps.title: Belgravia
steps.text: Robert Grosvenor, later 1st Marquess of Westminster, develops Belgravia in the 1820s.

steps.title: Capital goes abroad
steps.text: Annacis Island, Vancouver, is the first major overseas investment, followed by Australia, Asia (1994) and Europe (1996).

steps.title: Succession through trusts
steps.text: The 6th Duke dies; the estate is held by trustees, so the 7th Duke's inheritance does not trigger a 40% charge on its full value.

source.label: Chartered Institute of Taxation — Behind the headlines on the Duke and all that money

steps.title: Norway buys a quarter of Mayfair
steps.text: Norges Bank pays £304m for 24.99% of the Mayfair partnership; Grosvenor keeps control and management.

steps.title: Today: trusts, a £9.5bn platform, a £9.7bn Rich List figure
steps.text: Grosvenor Group is wholly owned by the Trustees of the Grosvenor Trusts; it reports shareholders' funds of £4.16bn and £9.5bn of assets under management, while the Rich List values the family at £9.677bn.

trails.title: From monastic land to the Bedford Estates: a Dissolution fortune
trails.summary: The Russells were given three monasteries in thirteen years and married a second Dissolution fortune, Bloomsbury. Leasehold squares turned both into ground rent; selling early in the death-duty era shrank the London estate, which survives as c. 20 acres beside Woburn.

steps.title: Tavistock Abbey
steps.text: Henry VIII grants the dissolved Tavistock Abbey to John Russell, courtier and later Earl of Bedford.

source.label: UCL Bloomsbury Project — Estates in Bloomsbury

steps.title: Wriothesley takes Bloomsbury
steps.text: Thomas Wriothesley, later Earl of Southampton, acquires Bloomsbury at the Dissolution.

source.label: UCL Bloomsbury Project — Estates in Bloomsbury

steps.title: Woburn and Covent Garden
steps.text: Woburn Abbey (1547) and Westminster Abbey's 'convent garden' (1552) follow; Covent Garden's piazza is later built on lease.

source.label: Wikipedia — Andrew Russell, 15th Duke of Bedford

steps.title: Bloomsbury by marriage
steps.text: Rachel Wriothesley marries William, Lord Russell; Bloomsbury joins the Russell estates.

source.label: UCL Bloomsbury Project — Estates in Bloomsbury

steps.title: Squares and leases
steps.text: Bedford Square and later Russell and Tavistock Squares are built on building leases, producing ground rents for the dukes.

source.label: UCL Bloomsbury Project — Estates in Bloomsbury

steps.title: Covent Garden sold
steps.text: The 11th Duke, selling ahead of rising death duties, completes the Covent Garden sale to Sir Thomas Beecham.

steps.title: Today: c. 20 acres and Woburn
steps.text: The Bedford Estates keep c. 20 of Bloomsbury's original 112 acres and the Woburn estate; the Rich List puts the Duke at £882m.

trails.title: From the Conqueror's demesne to offshore wind: the Crown's land
trails.summary: Land William I kept in 1066 became the royal demesne, was swollen by duchies, forfeitures and monastic seizures, and was handed to Parliament in 1760 as the Crown Estate. Today its seabed monopoly earns offshore-wind fees, and its profits set the monarchy's public funding.

steps.title: Conquest
steps.text: William I takes the lands of Harold and the English lords who fought against him.

steps.title: Land of the King
steps.text: Domesday records the royal demesne, estimated at about a fifth of England's recorded land.

steps.title: Lancaster joins the Crown
steps.text: Henry IV brings the Duchy of Lancaster, which is kept separate as the sovereign's private estate.

steps.title: Monastic seizures, then grants
steps.text: Henry VIII takes the monasteries' estates and grants or sells most of them to families such as the Russells and Herberts.

steps.title: Surrender to Parliament
steps.text: George III gives the hereditary Crown revenues to the Treasury for a Civil List: the origin of the Crown Estate.

source.label: GOV.UK — Crown Estate annual report 2025 to 2026

steps.title: Offshore wind windfall
steps.text: Round 4 option fees lift net revenue profit to £1.15bn in 2024/25, mostly from seabed leasing.

source.label: Baird Maritime — Crown Estate reports profit of £1.15bn led by offshore wind

steps.title: Today: £16.7bn of public Crown land, £680m of private royal wealth
steps.text: The Crown Estate's net asset value reaches £16.7bn while its revenue profit falls to £487m; the King's personal wealth is listed at £680m.
